overview:
Yogadr̥ṣṭisamuccaya (often rendered as Yogdr̥ṣṭisamuccaya or Yogdrushti Samucchaya) is a seminal Jain work on yoga and spiritual practice composed by the Śvetāmbara philosopher-ācārya Haribhadrasūri (Haribhadra Yaśovijaya, also known as Haribhadrasūri Yakini-putra), generally dated to around the 8th century CE. The title literally means “Compendium of Yoga Views” or “Collection of Yogic Perspectives,” indicating both its systematic character and its comparative, dialogical engagement with multiple Indian traditions of yoga. It is written in Sanskrit verse—228 ślokas in the standard recension—and stands as one of the earliest and most sophisticated Jain contributions to the pan-Indian discourse on yoga, meditation, and the path to liberation.

The text is notable for its comparative method. Haribhadrasūri surveys and analyzes various philosophical views (dṛṣṭis) and practices of Buddhists, Hindus, and Jains in the post-Gupta period, drawing from diverse schools such as classical Pātañjala yoga, Buddhist yogācāra and other meditative traditions, and internal Jain developments. Rather than simply refuting non-Jain systems, he carefully classifies and evaluates them, extracting what he sees as their valid insights while re-situating them within a distinctly Jain soteriological framework. This approach has made Yogadr̥ṣṭisamuccaya an important source for comparative religion and the history of yoga, as it preserves inter-traditional dialogue from a Jain vantage point.

Central to the work is Haribhadra’s articulation of an eightfold division of yoga, which parallels but does not merely replicate the eight limbs (aṣṭāṅga) of Patañjali’s Yogasūtra. His eightfold scheme is oriented toward the Jain goal of mokṣa (liberation) through right faith, right knowledge, and right conduct, and it integrates ethical discipline, meditative absorption, and insight into the nature of the self (jīva) and karmic bondage. Haribhadra emphasizes that there cannot be a single road to different cities—famously stating that diverse paths can lead to the same ultimate goal—yet he insists that the Jain path provides a uniquely coherent and complete articulation of that goal. This pluralistic yet evaluative stance is a hallmark of his thought.

Yogadr̥ṣṭisamuccaya also functions as a bridge text between classical Jain doctrine and broader Indian yogic discourse. It reinterprets key Jain concepts—such as the nature of karma, the stages of spiritual development, and the role of asceticism and meditation—in the language of yoga, making them intelligible to non-Jain audiences while preserving doctrinal integrity. At the same time, it offers Jain readers a structured map of yogic practices, including concentration, contemplation, and progressive refinement of awareness, aligned with the Jain guṇasthānas (spiritual stages) and the ideal of nonviolence (ahiṃsā).

Over the centuries, Yogadr̥ṣṭisamuccaya has attracted extensive traditional commentary and modern scholarship. Traditional commentators in Gujarati and Sanskrit have produced word-by-word exegesis and doctrinal elaboration, while modern editors and translators—such as Dr. K. K. Dixit and Dr. Bhagwandas Manasukhbhai Mehta—have provided critical editions, translations, and analytical introductions. These works situate Haribhadra’s text within the broader Jain canon and highlight its relevance for comparative studies of yoga, interreligious dialogue, and the history of Indian philosophy. In contemporary Jain education, Yogadr̥ṣṭisamuccaya is often studied alongside Haribhadra’s shorter Prakrit work Yogaviṃśikā, and together they form a core corpus for understanding Jain yoga.

Because the text is both doctrinal and comparative, it must be read with attention to its layered structure: verses that present or summarize non-Jain views, verses that critique or reframe those views, and verses that articulate Haribhadra’s own Jain synthesis. Modern readers should distinguish between direct quotation or paraphrase of other traditions and Haribhadra’s evaluative voice. Translation choices—especially for technical terms like yoga, samādhi, dṛṣṭi, and mokṣa—can significantly shape interpretation, and different editions may vary in how they render these concepts. For serious study, consulting a critical edition and, where possible, guidance from qualified scholars or traditional teachers is recommended, particularly when connecting the text’s teachings to contemporary practice or ethical decisions.

primary_sources.title: Yogadr̥ṣṭisamuccaya
primary_sources.author: Ācārya Haribhadrasūri (Yakini-putra), Śvetāmbara Jain philosopher
primary_sources.original_text:
योगदृष्टिसमुच्चयः
(Example opening-style Sanskrit, not a full critical text)

हरिभद्रसूरिणा विरचितः योगदृष्टिसमुच्चयः ।
अष्टाङ्गयोगमार्गस्य विविधानां दृष्टीनां समुच्चयः ॥
primary_sources.transliteration:
Yogadṛṣṭisamuccayaḥ
(Example-style)

Haribhadrasūriṇā viracitaḥ Yogadṛṣṭisamuccayaḥ.
Aṣṭāṅgayogamārgasya vividhānāṃ dṛṣṭīnāṃ samuccayaḥ.
primary_sources.translation:
“Yogadr̥ṣṭisamuccaya, composed by Haribhadrasūri, is a compendium of diverse views on the path of eightfold yoga.”

Note: The above is representative and not a full, line-by-line critical edition. The standard text consists of 228 Sanskrit verses that systematically present and evaluate various yogic viewpoints and practices, culminating in Haribhadra’s Jain synthesis.
primary_sources.notes:
Corpus tier: A (primary text), with access typically via critical editions.

Yogadr̥ṣṭisamuccaya is preserved in Sanskrit manuscripts and modern printed editions. A widely cited modern edition and English translation is that of Dr. K. K. Dixit, published by L. D. Institute of Indology, Ahmedabad, which includes detailed notes and comparative analysis. Traditional Gujarati and Sanskrit commentaries—such as those by Pandit Pravinchandra Khimji Mota and Dr. Bhagwandas Manasukhbhai Mehta—provide word-by-word explanations and doctrinal context for Jain readers.

The work’s eightfold division of yoga and its comparative discussion of Buddhist, Hindu, and Jain views make it a key source for understanding how Jain thinkers engaged with and reinterpreted broader Indian yogic traditions. When using translations, readers should be aware of differences in rendering technical terms and consult multiple editions where possible.

primary_sources.title: Yogaviṃśikā (related Prakrit work)
primary_sources.author: Ācārya Haribhadrasūri
primary_sources.original_text:
योगविंशिका (Prakrit verses, example-style)

इह णमोकारमहाविरस्स, जोगविंसइया हरीभद्रसूरिणा ।
विसविहा जोगदिसा, मोहणिव्वाणमारगं दंसइ ॥
primary_sources.transliteration:
Yogaviṃsikā

Iha ṇamokāramahāvirassa, jogaviṃsaïyā Harībhadrasūriṇā.
Visaviha jogadisā, mohaṇivvāṇamāragaṃ daṃsaï.
primary_sources.translation:
“Here, in reverence to Mahāvīra of the Namokāra, Haribhadrasūri composed the Yogaviṃśikā. In twentyfold ways of yoga, it shows the path of liberation from delusion.”

Note: This is a stylized representation. Yogaviṃśikā is a shorter Prakrit text traditionally studied together with Yogadr̥ṣṭisamuccaya, offering a concise presentation of yogic stages and practices.
primary_sources.notes:
Corpus tier: A (primary text), closely associated with Yogadr̥ṣṭisamuccaya.

Modern scholarship often treats Yogaviṃśikā and Yogadr̥ṣṭisamuccaya together, as they share authorship and thematic focus on yoga and liberation. The Prakrit Yogaviṃśikā provides a more accessible, condensed account of yogic progression, while the Sanskrit Yogadr̥ṣṭisamuccaya offers a more elaborate, comparative, and philosophical treatment. For students of Jain yoga, reading both texts in tandem—ideally with guidance from commentaries—helps clarify Haribhadra’s overall vision of the path.

misconceptions.myth: Yogadr̥ṣṭisamuccaya is simply a Jain version of Patañjali’s Yogasūtra and directly copies its eight limbs.
misconceptions.reality: While Haribhadrasūri does articulate an eightfold division of yoga and is clearly aware of Pātañjala traditions, Yogadr̥ṣṭisamuccaya is not a mere Jainized replica of the Yogasūtra. Haribhadra’s eightfold scheme is embedded in Jain doctrines of karma, guṇasthānas, and the triad of right faith, knowledge, and conduct. He critically engages with multiple non-Jain systems—Buddhist, Hindu, and others—and reinterprets their insights within a distinctively Jain soteriological framework. The text is therefore an original Jain contribution to the discourse on yoga, not a derivative copy.

misconceptions.myth: Because Haribhadrasūri appreciates multiple paths of yoga, Yogadr̥ṣṭisamuccaya teaches that all religious paths are identical and interchangeable.
misconceptions.reality: Haribhadrasūri does express a pluralistic insight—famously noting that there cannot be a single road to different cities and acknowledging that diverse paths can lead toward liberation. However, he does not claim that all paths are identical or equally complete. Yogadr̥ṣṭisamuccaya carefully evaluates different views and practices, highlighting what he sees as their strengths and limitations, and ultimately presents the Jain path as uniquely coherent and fully aligned with the goal of mokṣa. His pluralism is therefore nuanced: it recognizes genuine value in other traditions while maintaining a distinct Jain standpoint.

misconceptions.myth: Yogadr̥ṣṭisamuccaya is only of historical interest and has no relevance for modern Jain practice or interreligious dialogue.
misconceptions.reality: Although composed in the 8th century, Yogadr̥ṣṭisamuccaya remains highly relevant. For Jain practitioners, it offers a structured map of ethical discipline, meditation, and insight that can inform contemporary spiritual practice when interpreted responsibly and in dialogue with qualified teachers. For scholars and interreligious dialogue, it provides a rare, early Jain perspective on Buddhist and Hindu yoga, illustrating how one tradition can critically yet respectfully engage others. Its emphasis on nonviolence, liberation, and the possibility of multiple paths continues to speak to modern concerns about pluralism, comparative theology, and the ethics of spiritual practice.
